newsitem.title: USA: US jobless claims dip reopens tight labor question.
newsitem.headline: US jobless claims dip reopens tight labor question.

text.p: A sharp drop in new claims for unemployment insurance in the latest week has again raised the question of whether the U.S. labor market is tight enough to engender upward wage pressures -- and inflation -- down the road, analysts said.

"For starters, the drop in jobless claims serves as a good reminder that the issue of labor market tightness has not been resolved simply because of the payrolls drop in September," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets.
Economists had expected jobless claims in the week ended October 5 to rise a bit to 342,000 after totaling 340,000 in the previous week.
Instead, they fell to 319,000 from a revised 341,000 a week earlier.

Last Friday, the government reported that the number of jobs on U.S. non-farm payrolls dropped by 40,000 in September. Though some other aspects of the employment report were stronger than that number implied, the U.S. Treasury market rallied on the news.

"The 40,000 payroll jobs drop may not be representative (of the labor market)," said Karydakis. "The drop in (claims for state unemployment insurance) reopens the issue of how tight the labor market is. It casts the payroll part of the September employment report in a different light. We have quite a few signs that the labor market is still pretty tight."

David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc, said seasonal factors may have contributed to the fall in claims. However, overall, he said the report "adds to suspicions that the September non-farm payrolls drop was a bit of an aberration."
"We should get stronger non-farm payrolls growth in October," Sloan said.

The Treasury market, which has been in a nervous retreat since it rallied on Friday in reaction to the September employment report, opened lower on Thursday and lost further ground on the unexpected drop in new jobless claims.
But it seemed to stabilize at lower levels with the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond down 12/32 to 98-19/32, yielding 6.86 percent, an old resistance level that is now support.
Besides benefitting from some technical support, the market is seeing some caution before Friday's economic data.
The government reports the September Producer Price Index (PPI) and September retail sales data on Friday.
"The big numbers -- the PPI and retail sales -- are tomorrow," said Sloan. "No one will want to move that much before then."
"There is an expectation for an outsized increase in the PPI and retail sales are likely to be soft," said Karydakis.
"People will probably want to see what happens on Friday before they make a decision."
